blocks.content: Imagine you walk into a stranger's kitchen and someone hands you 45 minutes and says cook dinner. You would not grab a pan and start frying eggs immediately. You would first check what is actually in the fridge, how many people are eating, and whether anyone has a nut allergy. Only then would you decide what to cook.

A high level design interview works the exact same way. The prompt you get, design an e-commerce checkout, design a ride hailing app, design a chat system, is deliberately vague. It is not a trick question, it is an invitation to ask what is actually in the fridge before you start cooking.

This topic is the flagship overview for the whole System Design Interview Preparation module. Every other topic in this module, requirement clarification, capacity estimation, bottleneck identification, trade off justification, common mistakes, and case studies, is a deep dive into one specific phase of the flow this lesson lays out. Think of this as the map, and the rest of the module as the terrain.

blocks.title: What this lesson is not
blocks.content: This is not a lesson about how to design any particular system. It will not teach you how load balancers or databases work. It teaches you how to run the 45 to 60 minutes of the interview itself, the meta skill that determines whether all your technical knowledge actually lands.
1. Introduction

Most candidates walk into an HLD interview thinking the goal is to produce an impressive looking architecture diagram by the end. That is only half true. The interviewer is watching a process unfold in real time, how you think, what you ask, where you spend your minutes, and how you react when something does not fit. A clean diagram with no clarifying questions behind it is a red flag, not a win.

The good news is that this process is learnable and repeatable. Once you internalize the shape of the interview, you stop reacting to the prompt and start executing a plan. That is exactly what this topic gives you, a repeatable shape you can carry into any HLD interview regardless of the specific system you are asked to design.
2. The Shape of a Typical HLD Interview
blocks.text: 2. The Shape of a Typical HLD Interview

blocks.content: A standard HLD interview runs 45 to 60 minutes. That sounds like a lot until you realize a real system design could easily fill three hours of discussion. The constraint is the entire game. You are not being asked to design a complete system, you are being asked to demonstrate, in a tightly bounded window, that you know how to approach one.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396372738-950459250.png
blocks.alt: A rough time budget flowing across clarify scope, capacity estimate, high level design, deep dive, trade offs, and wrap up

blocks.content: The exact minutes flex depending on the interviewer and the problem, but a reasonable default budget looks like this.

{"headers":["Phase","Rough time","Primary goal"],"rows":[["Clarify requirements and scope","5 to 8 min","Agree on what you are actually building"],["Rough capacity estimation","5 min","Get a feel for scale, not exact numbers"],["Sketch a high level architecture","10 to 15 min","Get the core flow on the board"],["Drill into one or two components","10 to 15 min","Show depth where it matters"],["Discuss trade offs and bottlenecks","5 to 10 min","Show judgment, not just knowledge"],["Wrap up","5 min","Monitoring, scaling, and future considerations"]]}

blocks.title: This is a default, not a rulebook
blocks.content: Some interviewers will push you to spend twenty minutes on one component and skip the wrap up entirely. Follow their lead. The budget is a mental anchor for you, not a script the interviewer is obligated to follow.
2.1 Why a mental clock matters

Without some sense of the clock, it is very easy to spend eighteen minutes clarifying requirements because the conversation is comfortable, and then rush the entire architecture in the last ten minutes because you ran out of runway. Interviewers notice this. A design that trails off unfinished leaves a much worse impression than a slightly rougher design that reached a real conclusion.
You do not need a stopwatch on the table. A rough internal sense, roughly five minutes have passed, I should be moving toward scale numbers now, is enough to keep you on pace.
2.2 What happens if you blow the budget on one phase
blocks.text: 2.2 What happens if you blow the budget on one phase

blocks.content: If you notice you are ten minutes into what should have been a five minute capacity estimate, the fix is not to panic, it is to say so out loud. A simple line like let me lock in these rough numbers and move on to the design, we can come back to this if needed, resets the pace without any awkwardness. Interviewers respect a candidate who manages their own time more than one who needs to be redirected.
3. The Six Phases in Order

Every HLD interview, regardless of the specific prompt, moves through the same six phases in roughly the same order. Knowing this order in advance means you are never wondering what to do next, you are just executing.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396372738-926936196.png
blocks.alt: Six phases in sequence, clarify, estimate, sketch, drill down, trade offs, wrap up, with an optional loop back from trade offs to the sketch when something needs revisiting

blocks.content: 3.1 Clarify requirements and scope

You figure out what you are actually building and, just as importantly, what you are explicitly not building. This phase gets its own deep dive later in the module, but the short version is that a good scope statement removes ambiguity for both of you.
3.2 Rough capacity estimation

You put rough numbers on the problem, users, requests per second, storage growth, so that later design decisions have something concrete to justify them against. This is covered in full in the capacity estimation topic. The point here is only that it happens right after scoping, before you draw a single box.
3.3 Sketch a high level architecture

You put the core components on the board, client, some kind of API layer, a datastore, whatever the problem actually needs, and you connect them with the one or two flows that matter most. This is intentionally a rough sketch, not a finished blueprint. Precision comes in the next phase.
3.4 Drill into one or two components
blocks.text: 3.4 Drill into one or two components

blocks.content: You cannot go deep on everything in fifteen minutes, so you pick the one or two components where the interesting decisions actually live and go deep there. Everything else stays at the sketch level.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396372738-117362380.png
blocks.alt: Choosing to go deep on one component with real trade offs instead of touching every component shallowly

blocks.content: A common instinct is to try to say something about every box on the board so nothing looks neglected. Resist it. A thin sentence about six components reads as surface knowledge. A real, reasoned discussion of one or two components reads as depth.
3.5 Discuss trade offs and bottlenecks

You name what breaks first as load grows, and what you gave up to get the properties you wanted elsewhere. This is where junior and senior answers diverge the most, and it gets its own dedicated topic later in this module.
3.6 Wrap up with monitoring, scaling, and future considerations
blocks.text: 3.6 Wrap up with monitoring, scaling, and future considerations

blocks.content: You close the loop. How would you know if this system was unhealthy in production. What would you change first if traffic grew ten times over. What did you deliberately leave out of scope that a real version of this system would eventually need.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396866291-23668859.png
blocks.alt: Monitoring, scaling plan, and future considerations all feeding into a short wrap up at the end of the interview

blocks.content: 4. The Single Biggest Mistake: Jumping Straight to Boxes
blocks.text: 4. The Single Biggest Mistake: Jumping Straight to Boxes

blocks.content: If there is one thing to take from this entire lesson, it is this. The single most common way candidates hurt themselves in an HLD interview is skipping straight to drawing boxes the moment they hear the prompt.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396375776-282077602.png
blocks.alt: Jumping straight to boxes without clarifying leads to a design built on wrong assumptions, while clarifying scope first leads to a design that matches the real problem

blocks.content: Here is the part that surprises people. The interviewer is forming their entire impression of you from how you handle ambiguity, not from how many buzzwords you can fit on the whiteboard. A candidate who rattles off sharding, caching, and message queues within the first two minutes, without ever asking who the users are or how many of them there are, has told the interviewer something important, and it is not a compliment.

blocks.title: Why this hurts you so much
blocks.content: A design built on wrong assumptions cannot be saved by good execution later. If you assume a system needs to serve 10 million users when the interviewer actually meant 10 thousand, every downstream decision, caching, sharding, replication, is now solving a problem that does not exist. Clarifying first is not a soft skill add on, it is the thing that makes the rest of your answer correct.
4.1 What clarifying actually sounds like

Good clarifying questions are short, specific, and show you already have a mental model of what matters. Vague questions like what should I design exactly signal the opposite. Aim for questions that narrow the problem fast.

["Who are the users, and roughly how many of them are we talking about","What is the one core action the system must support well","Are we designing for read heavy or write heavy traffic","Is strong consistency required, or is eventual consistency acceptable here","What is explicitly out of scope for this conversation"]
items: Who are the users, and roughly how many of them are we talking about
What is the one core action the system must support well
Are we designing for read heavy or write heavy traffic
Is strong consistency required, or is eventual consistency acceptable here
What is explicitly out of scope for this conversation

blocks.content: 4.2 A worked example: from vague prompt to scoped problem
blocks.text: 4.2 A worked example: from vague prompt to scoped problem

blocks.title: Turning design a URL shortener into a real scope
blocks.text: Interviewer: design a URL shortener. Candidate: before I sketch anything, a few quick questions. Roughly how many URLs get created per day, and how many redirects do we serve for each one created. Do links need to expire or ever be deleted. Do we need custom aliases, or is a random short code enough. Interviewer: assume 100 million redirects a day for every 1 million created, no custom aliases for now, links live forever. Candidate: great, that tells me this is heavily read skewed, so caching and fast lookups matter more than write throughput. I will keep that in mind for the architecture.

blocks.content: Notice what happened there. The candidate did not just collect facts, they immediately said out loud what the facts implied for the design. That single sentence, that tells me this is heavily read skewed, is doing more work than any buzzword could.
5. Narrating Your Plan Out Loud

One of the cheapest ways to build interviewer confidence costs you nothing technical at all. Before you have designed a single piece of the system, you can say out loud how you intend to spend the next 45 minutes.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396375777-916034293.png
blocks.alt: Stating your plan out loud lets the interviewer see structure, which builds confidence before any actual design exists

blocks.content: I want to spend a few minutes on requirements, then estimate rough scale, then sketch the core flow, and leave time to go deep on whichever piece turns out to be the most interesting. Does that sound reasonable to you?

That single sentence does three things at once. It shows you have a process instead of just reacting to the prompt. It invites the interviewer to redirect you early if they had something specific in mind. And it sets an expectation you can now be measured against, which, if you actually follow the plan, works entirely in your favor.
5.1 A sample opening exchange
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396375777-432673788.png
blocks.alt: A short sample exchange where the candidate clarifies scope before agreeing to sketch the matching flow for a ride hailing app

blocks.title: A realistic opening thirty seconds
blocks.text: Interviewer: design a ride hailing app. Candidate: before I start, who are we optimizing for, riders, drivers, or both, and is the core problem here the matching flow or something else like pricing. Interviewer: both, and focus on matching. Candidate: got it. I will clarify scale next, then sketch the matching flow, then we can go deep wherever it gets interesting.

blocks.content: 6. Junior vs Senior: What Actually Gets Evaluated
blocks.text: 6. Junior vs Senior: What Actually Gets Evaluated

blocks.content: The same prompt, given to a junior candidate and a senior candidate, is being scored against very different bars. Knowing which bar you are being held to changes how you should spend your time.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396375777-809836184.png
blocks.alt: The same prompt evaluated differently, junior candidates judged on producing a working design, senior candidates judged on sound trade offs and pushback

blocks.content: {"headers":["What junior candidates are judged on","What senior candidates are judged on"],"rows":[["Can you produce a working design at all","Do you make sound, justified trade offs"],["Do you know the standard building blocks","Do you push back on unclear or unrealistic requirements"],["Can you explain your own diagram clearly","Can you reason about what breaks first at scale"],["Do you follow a reasonable process","Do you know when a simple design beats a clever one"]]}

blocks.title: Do not over correct
blocks.content: If you are early career, you do not need to fake senior level trade off debates you have not actually developed judgment for yet. A clear, correct, well reasoned junior level answer beats a senior sounding answer that falls apart under a single follow up question.
6.1 Pushing back on unclear requirements

Senior candidates treat an unclear requirement as something to negotiate, not something to silently guess at. If the interviewer says the system needs to be real time, a senior answer asks what real time actually means here, under one second, under one hundred milliseconds, because the answer changes the entire architecture.
6.2 Reasoning about what breaks at scale
blocks.text: 6.2 Reasoning about what breaks at scale

blocks.content: Senior candidates do not just describe what their design does, they describe what happens to it under stress. What happens when one region goes down. What happens when a single customer sends ten times the expected traffic. That kind of forward reasoning is exactly what the bottleneck identification topic later in this module trains you to do on purpose.
7. Handling What You Don't Know

At some point in almost every HLD interview, you will get asked about something you genuinely do not know well. How a specific database indexes data internally, how a particular consensus protocol behaves during a network partition, something like that. What you do in that moment matters more than the gap itself.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396375778-573579454.png
blocks.alt: Admitting a knowledge gap and reasoning from first principles earns trust, while confidently guessing tends to unravel under a follow up question

blocks.content: Interviewers ask follow up questions precisely because a first answer can sound confident and still be wrong. A candidate who bluffs usually survives the first question and gets caught on the second. A candidate who is upfront about the gap, and then reasons through it out loud from first principles, almost always comes across better, even though they admitted not knowing something.

blocks.title: What honesty sounds like in practice
blocks.text: I have not worked deeply with that specific database's internals, so let me reason through what I would expect. If it uses a log structured merge tree, writes should be fast and cheap, but reads might need to check multiple levels, so I would expect read latency to be the thing to watch here.

blocks.title: Interviewers can tell
blocks.content: Most interviewers have run dozens of these interviews and have heard every kind of bluff. The tell is almost always a confident tone paired with an answer that gets vaguer the more specific the follow up question gets. Honest uncertainty followed by real reasoning reads as far more senior than a lucky guess.
